profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Phoenix - Deer Valley) is located at 1850 West Deer Valley Road, Phoenix, AZ 85027. The operator publishes a footprint of 109,476 square feet and 5.02 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including HITRUST CSF, PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, NIST 800-53, ITAR, SSAE 18. More than 125 data centers now operate in Maricopa County, making Phoenix the second-largest data center market in the country by some measures; Arizona Public Service (APS) has said it has received 19 gigawatts of electrical service requests from data centers and large commercial users it currently cannot serve, with individual requests now averaging about 500 megawatts each, equivalent to powering 500 large retail stores simultaneously, according to reporting on the utility's filings. Data center peak demand has been growing roughly 100 times faster than all other APS customer categories combined, and data centers were projected to represent 94% of all APS system energy demand growth between 2023 and 2025, even as average residential electricity use fell about 5% over the same period. APS has filed for a nearly 14% residential rate increase expected no earlier than July 2026, and SRP raised rates in November 2025, including a 50% increase in fixed monthly charges for single-family homes; APS spends roughly $2 billion annually on capital infrastructure. Community members, including Sun City retirees, have testified at Arizona Corporation Commission hearings about the strain of rising utility costs.

Phoenix adopted its first data-center-specific zoning framework in 2025, following Chandler's earlier lead among Valley cities; the city council made data centers a permitted use requiring a new Special Permit process, with noise mitigation required within 300 feet of residential areas, a minimum half-mile setback from high-capacity transit corridors, and architectural standards barring "large, monotonous, undifferentiated" facades, according to the city's Planning and Development Department. Planning and Development Director Josh Bednarek said the goal was to plan for data center growth responsibly rather than restrict it, while Mayor Kate Gallego called for a balanced approach that protects the grid and prioritizes job creation; the ordinance followed a Planning Commission hearing in June 2025 and applies citywide, including the Deer Valley corridor where this facility sits.

profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential - Denver - Aurora) is located at 11900 East Cornell Avenue, Building A, Aurora, CO 80014. The operator publishes a footprint of 171289 square feet and 6.75 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including HITRUST CSF, PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, NIST 800-53, ITAR, SSAE 18. This building sits in the Denver-Aurora corridor local reporting has dubbed "Data Center Row," which also includes a major QTS facility under construction in Aurora. Xcel Energy, the region's dominant utility, said in 2025 it was seeking to invest $22 billion to add 12 to 14 gigawatts of new generation and transmission capacity by 2040, driven substantially by data center demand; the utility reported pending data center applications for 5.8 gigawatts of electricity, nearly matching its entire existing 6.2-gigawatt Colorado generating capacity, with data center load projected to reach 8.5 gigawatts by 2040, per Colorado Sun's reporting. The Colorado Public Utilities Commission has voiced skepticism about the reliability of these forecasts, noting that between October and May alone, seven data center prospects representing 4 gigawatts withdrew requests while more than a dozen new prospects totaling 3.5 gigawatts filed applications, with regulators and consumer advocates warning that ratepayers could face stranded-asset costs if projected demand fails to materialize.

The QTS facility anchoring the Aurora side of "Data Center Row" is planned at 177 megawatts of capacity on 80 acres at the I-70/C-470 interchange, positioned to become Xcel Energy's largest industrial customer in Colorado, on par with Evraz Rocky Mountain Steel in Pueblo, a marked shift from Xcel's historical major customers in mining and manufacturing, per Colorado Sun's 2023 reporting. That single campus is expected to require 160 megawatts of peak load delivered via a $28 million high-voltage transmission line, ramping up over roughly a decade, with Xcel anticipating similar-scale loads from other emerging data center customers in the region. For QTS, electricity was reported to represent about 40% of operating costs, underscoring why competitive utility rates were central to the Aurora site decision, a dynamic shared broadly across Colorado's Front Range data center corridor.

profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Fort Lauderdale) is located at 5301 NW 33rd Avenue, Fort Lauderdale, FL 33309. The operator publishes a footprint of 64164 square feet and 3.15 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, HIPAA, ISO 27001, SSAE 18. Duke Energy, a major Florida utility, announced a five-year, $103 billion growth plan in 2026 that it expects to grow further, targeting 20 gigawatts of new generation over the coming decade; the company said AI data center customers including Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta were a primary driver alongside population growth of roughly 200,000 people a year into its service territory and grid-hardening investment against severe weather, per Fortune's reporting. Duke CEO Harry Sideris said hyperscale data center customers are paying for their own dedicated infrastructure and that broader rate increases stem mainly from population growth and grid resilience work rather than data centers alone; in Florida specifically, Duke has been replacing wooden utility poles with steel and concrete as part of its storm-hardening strategy. About 60% of Duke's planned capital spending is allocated to new generation (gas turbines, solar, battery storage, and nuclear plant life extensions) and the remaining 40% to grid expansion and upgrades. Duke separately confirmed in 2025 that it was exploring building data centers of its own in Florida, according to WUSF's reporting.

Florida's data center sales-tax landscape changed materially in 2025: House Bill 7031, effective August 1, 2025, eliminated the state's sales-tax exemption on equipment, electricity, and construction materials for data centers with IT loads below 100 megawatts, preserving the exemption only for facilities at or above that threshold, with no grandfather clause for existing sub-100 MW facilities, per Ryan LLC's tax-advisory analysis. All of Flexential's Florida buildings, including this one, operate well under that 100 MW threshold, meaning they and their colocation tenants would no longer qualify for the exemption on new purchases made after the effective date, a shift that has been reported to create potential retroactive tax exposure and pressure toward lease renegotiations for smaller colocation operators statewide.

The property was originally built out by InetU, founded around 1996 and acquired by ViaWest in 2015; ViaWest merged with Peak 10 in 2017 to form Flexential in 2018. Pennsylvania's data center market overall trails the major East Coast hubs of Northern Virginia and the New York/New Jersey corridor, with the Lehigh Valley representing a smaller submarket than Philadelphia's own suburbs.

Pennsylvania's data center sales-tax exemption, established in 2016 as a refund capped at $5 million and restructured in 2021 into an uncapped exemption with reduced state tracking ability, is now projected by the Shapiro administration to cost $188 million in the 2026-27 fiscal year, rising to $517 million by fiscal year 2031, with total losses since inception potentially reaching about $2 billion by mid-2031, according to Spotlight PA's reporting. Cryptocurrency miners were banned from the program in 2024. State Rep. Greg Vitali introduced a bill to repeal the exemption, but acknowledged uncertain prospects given Governor Shapiro's public support for the program; Shapiro's own budget proposal assumes the exemption continues, with conditional added benefits for developers meeting environmental and employment standards.

The operator publishes a footprint of 28,594 square feet and 2.8 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building. Published certifications and compliance attestations include PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, HIPAA, ISO 27001, SSAE 18.

Richmond is a secondary Virginia data center market compared with the dominant Northern Virginia/Loudoun County corridor, often called "Data Center Alley," which hosts a much larger concentration of hyperscale and colocation capacity. Richmond also hosts Meta's much larger Henrico County campus, documented elsewhere in this registry, a separate facility from Flexential's smaller colocation building. Dominion Energy Virginia serves both the Richmond and Northern Virginia markets and has been at the center of statewide debate over data center-driven transmission and generation investment, including the Schedule RF renewable tariff Dominion created for large data center customers.

Virginia's data center boom is reshaping statewide electricity rates directly relevant to this Richmond-area facility. In November 2026, the Virginia State Corporation Commission approved new Dominion Energy rates that will raise a typical residential bill by about $16 a month to roughly $165, while creating a new GS-5 rate class specifically for data centers effective January 1, 2027; Dominion's allowed profit margin was set at 9.8% versus the 10.4% it requested, and regulators approved $775.6 million of the roughly $1.2 billion Dominion sought, cutting about $350 million tied to speculative data center projects that had not reached firm commitments, according to Inside Climate News. Under the new rules, data center customers with 25 megawatts or more of demand must sign 14-year mandatory contracts, pay a minimum 85% of transmission and distribution costs and a minimum 60% of generation costs regardless of actual usage, post collateral upfront for grid upgrades, and pay exit fees if they later shop for alternative power. The Piedmont Environmental Council has criticized the deal, noting an estimated 61% of grid-upgrade costs still fall on ordinary ratepayers once a facility's 14-year contract term ends; Ohio's experience with similar minimum-payment provisions cut that state's pending data center interconnection requests from about 30 gigawatts to 13 gigawatts, a precedent Virginia regulators cited in weighing the new rate class.

The registry here tracks 43 Flexential facilities across fifteen states, Arizona, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nevada, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, and Virginia, a wide multi-region colocation footprint consistent with the ViaWest and Peak 10 predecessor geographies it was built from, Western states from ViaWest, Southeastern states from Peak 10.
